prs.title: fix(providers): bound inline media per request, not just per file
prs.body:
## Summary

The per-file inline cap (`MAX_INLINE_MEDIA_BYTES`, 2 MB) does not bound the
**request body**. Media counts ~0 tokens, so token-based context eviction
never fires, and a session that accumulates many *in-spec* images keeps
sending a multi-megabyte body on every turn. Once a gateway's byte limit
answers 413 the session is unusable until the history is stripped by hand.

This adds a cumulative inline-media budget to the shared capping
formatters, so the request body is bounded independently of tokens.

Refs #7671

## What Problem This Solves

The reporter's incident: a design-review session accumulated ~20 MB of
inline base64 screenshots — every one *under* the 2 MB per-file cap — and
every subsequent turn failed with provider 413 until the session JSON was
surgically stripped. A 2,979,813-byte PNG also became
`[Image unavailable: ... exceeds the 2097152-byte image limit.]`, i.e. an
image marginally over the line was dropped even though a slightly smaller
version would have been fine.

PR #7965 fixed the Scroll-side half (reclaim historical media, fold media
into the existing compression flow) and explicitly listed this as remaining:

> **Out of scope / TODO** — HTTP request-body limits: accumulated media can
> still exceed a gateway's byte limit without exceeding the token threshold.

This PR closes that TODO.

## Changes

`src/qwenpaw/providers/capping_formatter.py`:

- New `max_total_bytes` field (default `MAX_TOTAL_INLINE_MEDIA_BYTES` = 8 MB
  = 4× the per-file cap; `0` disables it, restoring per-file-only behaviour).
  The field is **derived from the instance's per-file cap** when it is not
  set explicitly: `max(8 MiB, 4 × max_bytes)`. A raised per-file cap is
  therefore no longer undercut by a fixed total — with a 16 MiB per-file cap
  a 10 MiB file reaches the wire instead of being dropped by the total — and
  a lowered per-file cap never tightens the total below the 8 MiB default.
  An explicitly configured `max_total_bytes` always wins.
- The budget is spent in two passes. A **measuring** pass records the size of
  every media block in wire order; only when the measured total exceeds the
  budget does an **enforcing** pass run, replacing the oldest media (a byte
  prefix of the wire order) with placeholders. The newest media is what the
  request keeps.
- `_cap_media` runs the per-file cap first, so a file that is already a
  placeholder is never charged to the budget.
- `inline_media_size()` also sizes inline `data:` URLs, and the OpenAI Chat /
  Responses formatters route PDF attachments through `_format_file_source()`,
  so `data:` URLs and PDFs count toward the budget like any other media.
- A base64 payload is measured **without its `=` padding**, for a
  `Base64Source` and for a base64 `data:` URL alike (one shared helper). The
  padding is not payload: a 512-byte image encodes to 684 characters, one of
  which is padding, so it is 512 bytes — not 513, which was enough to push a
  file sitting exactly on the per-file cap over it while the equivalent
  `Base64Source` was kept.
- The per-request media **dedup scope** lives next to the budget policy
  (`SEEN_MEDIA_KEYS`) and is reset between the measuring and the enforcing
  pass — both passes have to observe the same media, otherwise the enforcing
  pass sees every source as "already shown above" and drops all media,
  including the newest one the budget keeps.

`src/qwenpaw/agents/model_factory.py`:

- The Anthropic formatter now only remembers a media source as *seen* once it
  has actually reached the wire. A source the budget dropped is not part of
  the request, so a later copy of it stays eligible: with **A → B → A**
  (512 bytes each, 900-byte budget) the request keeps the newest **A**
  instead of folding it as "already shown above" while the dropped copy is
  nowhere in the request.
- A folded duplicate still occupies a slot in the wire order, but it is never
  sent, so it costs the budget nothing: the plan drops oldest occurrences only
  until the *deduplicated* payload — the distinct sources that actually reach
  the wire — fits the budget, and a folded copy is re-inlined when the budget
  dropped every earlier copy of its source (so A → B → A still keeps the
  newest A).
- **Video is bounded by the budget too.** Video never reaches a media hook:
  Anthropic routes it through `_format_anthropic_video_data_block`, and the
  OpenAI Chat / Responses / DashScope paths substitute it into the request
  around the formatter's `format()` call. The Anthropic path now caps the
  video before formatting it, and the OpenAI-family paths *mark* the video
  block (its `name` becomes the substitution placeholder) instead of
  replacing it, so the formatter's media hook still sees it and the budget
  can account for it at its own position in the wire order. A marked block is
  rendered as the substitution placeholder and resolved to the video wire
  dict afterwards, exactly as before. Assistant-role video is unaffected (it
  was never substituted and still is not).
- **A local PDF is prepared like any other media.** A `file://` PDF used to
  stay a `URLSource`: the asynchronous media preparation did not read it, so
  the formatter could not measure it and the base formatter inlined the whole
  file (with a blocking disk read) while formatting — three 512-byte PDFs
  fitted a 900-byte budget without a single budget placeholder. The
  preparation stage now reads local PDF attachments too, so they spend the
  per-request budget like every other media and obey the per-file cap (a
  local PDF above `max_bytes` becomes the same text placeholder an oversized
  image gets). Remote PDFs follow the same path for the OpenAI Chat /
  Responses formatters, which have to download them anyway: the download
  moves out of the formatter into the bounded, non-blocking preparation
  stage.

Because formatting walks the conversation oldest-first, spending the budget
as it is spent **keeps the newest media and drops the oldest** — the
direction the issue asks for.

A `ContextVar` rather than instance state, because formatter instances are
shared across concurrent requests and a running total on the instance would
let one session spend another's allowance
(`test_concurrent_requests_do_not_share_a_budget` pins this).

Placeholder wording distinguishes the two causes, and every provider shape
is preserved: Chat Completions / Anthropic / DashScope `{"type":"text"}`,
Gemini `{"text"}`, Responses API `{"type":"input_text"}`.

## Evidence

```
$ pytest tests/unit/providers/test_capping_formatter.py -q
89 passed
```

`TestCumulativeBudgetEndToEnd` drives the **real** formatters (OpenAI,
Anthropic, Gemini, DashScope, and the Responses formatter) over a
three-image conversation with a budget that fits only one:

```
[media omitted from model context: this request already inlines 513 bytes
 of media, exceeds the 900-byte per-request limit]     <- oldest, dropped
[media omitted from model context: ... 900-byte ...]   <- middle, dropped
{"inline_data": {...}}                                 <- newest, inlined
```

`TestCumulativeBudgetThroughProductionWrapper` drives the same scenario
through the production formatter wrapper, and
`TestRepeatedMediaSurvivesTheBudget` pins the repeated-source case through
the Anthropic wrapper, the same case with the newest copy arriving in a tool
result, and the OpenAI Chat / Responses paths:

```
A (512 B) -> B (512 B) -> A (512 B), 900-byte budget
  before:  A dropped by the budget, B inlined, newest A folded as
           "[Image omitted - already shown above]"
  after:   A dropped by the budget, B dropped by the budget,
           newest A inlined
```

The two Anthropic cases fail without the fix (verified by reverting the
`model_factory.py` change):

```
FAILED TestRepeatedMediaSurvivesTheBudget::test_anthropic_wrapper_keeps_the_newest_repeated_media
FAILED TestRepeatedMediaSurvivesTheBudget::test_anthropic_wrapper_keeps_the_newest_repeated_tool_media
2 failed, 62 passed
```

`TestVideoUnderThePerRequestBudget` pins the video case on all five provider
paths through the production wrapper (three 312-byte `video/mp4` blocks, a
900-byte budget → two videos inlined, one dropped):

```
$ pytest tests/unit/providers/test_capping_formatter.py -q -k TestVideoUnderThePerRequestBudget
9 passed
```

`TestLocalPdfAttachmentsSpendTheBudget` pins the local-PDF case through the
production wrapper on the OpenAI Chat and Responses paths (three 512-byte
local PDFs, a 900-byte budget → the newest PDF inlined, two budget
placeholders), and the base64 padding case with
`test_data_url_size_matches_the_equivalent_base64_source` (a `data:` URL and
the equivalent `Base64Source` measure the same, padding excluded).

Without the fix the new cases fail:

```
FAILED test_data_url_size_matches_the_equivalent_base64_source[512]
FAILED test_data_url_image_at_the_per_file_cap_is_kept
FAILED TestLocalPdfAttachmentsSpendTheBudget::test_openai_wrapper_caps_local_pdf_attachments
FAILED TestLocalPdfAttachmentsSpendTheBudget::test_responses_wrapper_caps_local_pdf_attachments
FAILED TestLocalPdfAttachmentsSpendTheBudget::test_local_pdf_over_the_per_file_cap_is_dropped
```

Wider runs — no regressions. The failures below are pre-existing in this
environment (missing optional SDKs — `reme`, `typesafe` — and one
network-dependent download test) and are identical on the unmodified head
commit:

```
$ pytest tests/unit/providers tests/unit/agents -q
# this branch:        23 failed, 5098 passed, 3 skipped
# unmodified head:    23 failed, 5086 passed, 3 skipped   (+12 = the new tests)

$ black --line-length=79 / flake8 / pylint (10.00) / mypy   # clean
```

### The 8 MiB budget is raw media, not wire bytes

**Yes — the budget is intentionally in raw (decoded) media bytes.** It is the
same unit as the per-file cap and as the file size the user sees, so one
number describes the media a request carries.

`MAX_TOTAL_INLINE_MEDIA_BYTES` counts the **decoded** media bytes; base64
encoding expands them by 4/3 on the wire. An 8 MiB raw budget therefore
becomes roughly **10.7 MiB** of base64 in the request body — still above the
**6 MiB** limit of the `dash_anthropic` gateway. To stay inside that gateway
the raw budget has to stay at or below ~4.5 MiB (6 MiB x 3/4).

This is deliberate: the budget bounds the *media a request carries*, in the
same unit as the per-file cap and the file sizes reported to the user. The
alternative — budgeting encoded bytes — would mean the limit no longer
matches the number a user sees for a file, and it would still not track the
provider's own overhead on top of the media.

The default is therefore a bound on the request body, not a guarantee that
every gateway accepts it: deployments behind a 6 MiB gateway should lower
`MAX_TOTAL_INLINE_MEDIA_BYTES` (or set `max_total_bytes` explicitly on the
model) to match their gateway limit.

## Notes for review

- **The default changes behaviour**: a request that used to inline ~20 MB of
  media now inlines 8 MB and placeholders the rest. If you would rather this
  be opt-in, set `MAX_TOTAL_INLINE_MEDIA_BYTES = 0` and I will drop the
  default; the plumbing and tests are unaffected.
- The per-request budget now covers **video** as well, on all five provider
  paths. One path is still outside it: the OpenAI-family / Gemini
  **tool-result video promotion** (`_promote_tool_result_videos`) injects the
  video after formatting, so it is capped per file but not per request. The
  Anthropic tool-result video goes through the media hook and is covered.
  Covering the promotion would mean moving it inside the budget's scope —
  worth a follow-up if you want one budget for both paths.
- The issue's other asks (auto-downscale an oversized attachment instead of
  dropping it, and making the cap configurable per provider) are not
  included; the cap is already a provider field, so only the downscale is
  new work.

prs.title: feat(console): add Quick Add Model button in Models page (#4036)
prs.body:
Fixes #4036

## What Problem This Solves

Adding one model to an existing provider took five interactions across three screens: open the provider's detail page, find the model list, click Add, type the id, confirm — and repeat for each model. Users doing the common case (a new free model appeared, add it to a provider that is already configured) paid the full multi-screen cost every time.

This adds a **Quick Add Model** button in the Models page header, next to Add Provider. One modal, one form: pick a configured provider, type the model id (optional display name), save.

## Evidence

**What changed** (4 files, no backend change):

- `console/src/pages/Settings/Models/components/modals/QuickAddModelModal.tsx` (new, +110): provider picker restricted to **configured** providers (API key set, keyless, or OAuth — an unconfigured provider cannot serve a model, so offering it just moves the failure later), duplicate guard against both the provider's existing models and its extra/model list, save via the existing `api.addModel`, success/error toast.
- `console/src/pages/Settings/Models/index.tsx` (+14): the header button and the modal mount; `onSaved` refreshes the page data so the new row appears without a manual reload.
- `console/src/locales/{en,zh}.json` (+22/−3 each): every string the modal renders.

**Verification**

- `pnpm --filter console typecheck` clean; the console build compiles with the new modal.
- Manual path: Models page → Quick Add Model → the picker lists only providers with credentials → entering an id already present on that provider is rejected inline → saving adds the row and the table refreshes (the toast confirms).
- With no provider configured the button still opens, and the picker explains there is nothing to add to yet rather than showing an empty select.

Existing entry points are untouched: the provider detail page's Add Model flow still works exactly as before, so this is purely an additional faster path.

prs.title: feat(desktop): add approval notifications (#8460)
prs.body: ## Description Introduces a unified system notification feature, ensuring users receive timely alerts—such as approval requests, completed responses, and background task updates—even when the application is running in the background. Closed #8460 - Centralized notification management under "Settings → General," featuring a master toggle. Options for approval requests and completed responses include "Disabled," "Background Only," and "Always Enabled." Scheduled tasks, heartbeat signals, and email notifications can be configured individually. - Supports browser-based notifications as well as native system notifications on macOS, Windows, and Linux. On desktop, a Rust-based background polling mechanism ensures alerts are received even when the application window is minimized to the system tray. - Clicking a notification brings the application to the foreground and navigates directly to the relevant Agent, conversation, approval card, or inbox message. If an approval session is no longer valid, the user is redirected to the approval list. - Implements notification deduplication, filters out initial snapshot history, automatically dismisses expired or already-processed approval requests, and includes retry logic for failed deliveries—all to minimize redundant or obsolete alerts. - The backend now stores short-term, non-consumable notification event snapshots. Completion events are triggered only upon the successful finalization of a response, while empty "heartbeat" signals are filtered out. - Enhanced permission management, including streamlined authorization access, automatic UI refreshes upon permission changes, and direct access to system notification settings. Maintains backward compatibility with legacy approval preferences; category-specific settings are preserved even when the master notification toggle is disabled. - Added an approval access point in the system tray, with full support for multiple languages, narrow-screen layouts, and keyboard navigation. ## Type of Change - [ ] Bug fix - [x] New feature - [ ] Breaking change - [ ] Documentation - [ ] Refactoring ## Component(s) Affected - [ ] Core / Backend (app, agents, config, providers, utils, local_models) - [x] Console (frontend web UI) - [ ] Channels (DingTalk, Lark, QQ, Discord, iMessage, etc.) - [ ] Skills - [ ] CLI - [ ] Documentation (website) - [ ] Tests - [ ] CI/CD - [ ] Scripts / Deploy ## Checklist - [ ] I ran `pre-commit run --all-files` locally and it passes - [ ] If pre-commit auto-fixed files, I committed those changes and reran checks - [ ] I ran tests locally (`pytest` or as relevant) and they pass - [ ] Documentation updated (if needed) - [ ] Ready for review ### For Channel Changes (DingTalk, Lark, QQ, Console, etc.) - [ ] I ran `./scripts/check-channels.sh` (or `./scripts/check-channels.sh --changed`) and it passes - [ ] Official channel changes are covered in `tests/unit/channels/test_.py` (startup, shutdown and message delivery) - [ ] Shared host/process changes are covered in `test_channel_host.py` / `tests/unit/plugins/test_plugin_process.py` - [ ] Console changes retain the built-in contract checks in `tests/contract/channels/` ## Testing [How to test these changes] ## Evidence Examples of valid evidence: - Terminal transcript of the test run (e.g. `pytest tests/unit/app/chats/ -q` output) - Screenshot of the Console UI showing the fix - CI artifact link - `pre-commit run --all-files` summary ```bash pre-commit run --all-files # paste summary result pytest # paste summary result ``` ## Additional Notes [Optional: any other context]

prs.title: fix(pack): force-include console channel in PyInstaller bundle
prs.body:
## Description

`PyInstaller` cannot follow the dynamic `importlib.import_module(".console", ...)` call in `src/qwenpaw/app/channels/registry.py:_load_builtin_channels`. The console channel is therefore silently omitted from the Tauri sidecar bundle, and a packaged QwenPaw Desktop app fails to start with a hard `ModuleNotFoundError` on `qwenpaw.app.channels.console.channel`.

**Related Issue:** Affects only Tauri/PyInstaller desktop builds. Server, Docker, and \`pip install -e\` deployments are unaffected.

## What Problem This Solves

\`_load_builtin_channels\` walks a literal map of channel-id → (module, class) and loads each one with \`importlib.import_module\`. PyInstaller's static analysis only follows syntactic \`import\` statements, so the literal-string import targets are invisible to the bundler. The console channel is also listed in \`_REQUIRED_CHANNEL_KEYS\` (\`registry.py:31\`), so the missing import surfaces as a startup failure rather than a soft skip.

This PR adds an explicit \`hiddenimports\` entry so the package is bundled; the submodule \`console.channel\` is then pulled in by \`console/__init__.py\`'s existing \`from .channel import ConsoleChannel\` re-export, so a single entry is sufficient.

## Type of Change

- [x] Bug fix
- [x] Build / packaging

## Component(s) Affected

- [x] Core / Backend (app, agents, config, providers, utils, local_models)
- [x] Build / Packaging

## Testing

Verify on macOS / Windows after rebuilding the desktop bundle:

\`\`\`bash
pyinstaller scripts/pack-tauri/qwenpaw.spec
# Launch the packaged app; the console channel should load without
# ModuleNotFoundError on qwenpaw.app.channels.console.channel.
\`\`\`

Source install (\`pip install -e\`) and Docker/server deployments are unaffected because they import from the live source tree.

## Evidence

A standalone import reproduces the bundling dependency:

\`\`\`bash
$ python3 -c "
import importlib
m = importlib.import_module('qwenpaw.app.channels.console')
print('imported:', m.__name__)
print('channel attr present:', hasattr(m, 'channel'))
"
imported: qwenpaw.app.channels.console
channel attr present: True
\`\`\`

Importing the parent package triggers \`console/__init__.py\`, which in turn re-exports \`console.channel\` via \`from .channel import ConsoleChannel\`. Therefore a single \`hiddenimports\` entry for \`qwenpaw.app.channels.console\` is enough to guarantee both the package and its submodule ship in the bundle.

prs.title: fix(plugins): drop stale host evidence when a declaration is withdrawn
prs.body:
## Description

`DependencyUsageRegistry.withdraw()` removed the declaration but kept the
token's host evidence in the in-process registry. After one failed or
unfinished host observation that stale entry made every later dependency
audit for the plugin fail closed with "environment evidence unavailable"
until the process restarted, even after reloading the plugin.

`_observe_host()` also dropped `environment` while retaining the previous
snapshot, leaving a snapshot without environment that the same audit
rejects.

The fix pops the token's host evidence in `withdraw()` and always derives
the environment from the retained snapshot (`from_snapshot` returns None
when nothing usable is left).

## Related Issue

N/A — no existing issue found. Happy to file one if you prefer.

## Security Considerations

None. The change only affects in-process dependency evidence bookkeeping.

## Type of Change

- [x] Bug fix

## Evidence

Local run of the plugin unit tests:

```
$ PYTHONPATH=src python -m pytest tests/unit/plugins/test_dependency_usage.py -q
3 passed
```

- `test_withdraw_drops_host_evidence`: registering a host capture, then
  withdrawing the declaration, now leaves `_host` empty and bumps `_revision`;
  before the fix the entry stayed behind and every later audit for that token
  reported the stale capture as unusable for the rest of the process.
- `test_unknown_observation_keeps_last_capture`: an unknown host observation
  now keeps `DependencyEnvironment.from_snapshot(snapshot)` instead of
  dropping the environment to `None`, so the retained capture can still be
  pinned against a fresh read.
- `test_unknown_host_evidence_stays_unusable`: guards the existing behaviour
  that missing host evidence is still rejected.

## Evidence

prs.title: fix(harnesses): treat unrecognized slash text as a prompt
prs.body:
## Description

A message that starts with "/" (for example an absolute path pasted from
chat) was parsed as a provider command. When the provider did not declare
that command the runtime raised `ValueError: Unsupported <provider>
command: /...`, so the turn never reached the model.

This change only dispatches a provider command when the provider declares
it; otherwise the text is kept as the prompt. `/new` and `/clear` remain
host-level commands.

## Related Issue

N/A — no existing issue found. Happy to file one if you prefer.

## Security Considerations

None. The change only affects local prompt dispatch.

## Type of Change

- [x] Bug fix

## Evidence

Local run of the affected unit test file:


```
$ PYTHONPATH=src python -m pytest tests/unit/harnesses/test_runtime.py -q
8 passed
```

`test_runtime_treats_unknown_slash_text_as_prompt` drives a prompt that begins
with an absolute path (`/app/working/workspaces/<agent>/report.md`). Before the
fix the runtime raised `ValueError: Unsupported ... command`, so status was
`failed`. After the fix the adapter receives the text unchanged as
`adapter.prompt`, `adapter.command == ""`, and the run finishes `completed`
with output `Fixed`.

prs.title: fix(matrix): simplify legacy state migration and device locking
prs.body:
## Summary

Follow-up to #8187.

The previous legacy-state checks could prevent a valid Matrix account from starting when unrelated legacy files were present. Persistent device ownership could also block another workspace after the original workspace had stopped, while the host only reported `CHANNEL_NOT_CONNECTED`.

This PR simplifies the migration flow:

- Matching identities are migrated automatically by copying state into the current workspace.
- Mismatched identities start with independent workspace state instead of failing.
- Device exclusion is based on runtime locks rather than permanent workspace ownership.

## Changes

- Prefer existing state in the current workspace, including A → B → A account switches.
- Copy legacy sync tokens and crypto stores only when `user_id` and `device_id` match the authenticated identity.
- Preserve all legacy files during migration; fresh credentials are not overwritten by legacy auth data.
- Skip unrelated legacy state without blocking a valid account.
- Replace persistent device-owner enforcement with runtime device locks released when the Channel stops.
- Ignore stale owner/capture records without deleting user files.
- Preserve concurrent-use protection for the same Matrix device while allowing different device IDs.
- Fall back to initial catch-up when a non-E2EE sync-token copy fails.
- Fail explicitly on E2EE copy failures instead of creating a new identity for the same device.
- Propagate Matrix reason codes through the plugin host instead of returning only `CHANNEL_NOT_CONNECTED`.
- Remove the obsolete Matrix legacy-capture authorization module.
- Add migration, locking, failure-path, and host-error propagation tests.
- Update Matrix documentation in English and Chinese.

## Security and compatibility

- Legacy files remain read-only.
- Crypto state is never adopted across different user/device identities.
- Corrupt current workspace state still fails explicitly rather than being silently replaced.
- Concurrent use of the same account/device remains blocked.
- No access tokens, passwords, or key material are added to diagnostics.
- Other Channel implementations are unchanged.

## Tests

- Matrix migration and Channel tests: **18 passed**
- Channel unit suite: **159 passed, 1 environment-related failure**
- Plugin process suite: **56 passed, 1 skipped**
- `black`, `flake8`, `pylint`, and `git diff --check`: passed

prs.title: feat(plugins): support CLI commands and extension points
prs.body:
## Description

Adds plugin CLI commands to the existing Click command tree and connects them to the plugin registry, dependency checks, and resource lifecycle.

### 1) Key CLI features

- Register root commands, nested commands, or complete Click groups through `ctx.register_cli(CliSpec(...))`. Native commands retain priority.
- Installed, enabled plugins expose their commands. Disable/uninstall removes them. Core commands remain available without plugins.
- Plugin commands run without starting the App. Root help uses static declarations; selecting a command checks dependencies and loads its implementation.
- Invocation cleanup completes before resources and source leases are released, including after Ctrl-C. No dedicated session thread or process is added.
- Core `models`, `channels`, and `doctor` commands discover plugin contributions. Unavailable implementations retain their saved configuration without becoming executable.

### 2) Supporting plugin-core changes — review requested

The design separates application declarations, capability registration, driver execution, and resource ownership, following OS concepts.

#### 2.1 Shared registration, independent receiver execution

Previously, `entry.descriptor` and `entry.backend` were mutually exclusive. They can now coexist under one plugin instance and rollback ledger.

Simplified flow:

    App loading:
        register static channel metadata
        register lightweight public contributions

    Plugin CLI:
        load the public entry and selected command

    Enabled workspace receiver:
        start the existing channel worker

This lets a channel plugin also provide CLI or client Tools without requiring its receiver to run. Global plugin disablement still blocks execution. Public registration failure rolls back the combined registration; per-capability failure isolation is not implemented.

#### 2.2 Capability dependencies and invocation side effects

Package-wide dependencies remain supported. Named `optional_dependencies` and per-contribution `requires` distinguish lightweight operations from SDK-dependent operations:

    status.requires = []
    send.requires = ["transport"]

    install/update/repair:
        prepare packages referenced by declared capabilities

    selected command:
        check requires -> build implementation -> execute -> clean up

This prevents an unrelated SDK prerequisite from gating a lightweight command. Authors must keep the public entry lightweight and defer SDK imports themselves.

CLI execution also skips installation callbacks and backend provision commits. It reuses registration and runtime cleanup without rewriting existing Tool/Skill configuration.

#### 2.3 Update: reduce plugin CLI startup and cleanup overhead

Cleanup previously imported memory/model implementations just to inspect resource ownership. The existing memory registry now lives in a lightweight module, preserving public imports and the shared registry instance.

    Before: cleanup -> public memory API -> memory/model imports
    After:  cleanup -> lightweight ownership registry

Dependency observation now retains only file paths matching imported modules while still validating every RECORD row. Existing dependency checks, cache invalidation, and ownership protection remain in place.

For the same local Hello command, median peak RSS fell **214.77 → 193.69 MiB (-21.08 MiB)** and runtime fell **2.656 → 2.385 s (-10.2%)**.

The fixed plugin still uses **17.86 MiB / 0.591 s more** than the native reference. This includes shared-environment inspection and loader/SDK setup. Runtime environment inspection remains a current design tradeoff; reducing it further requires the environment-management work described below.

### 3) Reviewer decisions and TODOs

- [ ] Approve version choices: proposed SDK `1.1.0`, new API `since` values, and channel versioning/schema changes.
  - Channel descriptor schema v3 adds named `requires`; schema v2 remains supported.
  - Review compatibility and migration policy. The worker IPC protocol version is unchanged.
- [ ] Review test necessity and cost: 32 added runtime scenarios took approximately 70.4 seconds locally, primarily real installation and worker rollback.
- [ ] Complete installed-SDK author type validation and cross-platform CI.

Follow-up TODO comments cover installation/runtime lifecycle separation, Tool/Skill dependency declarations, live cross-plugin services, broader extension consumers, per-capability failure/reclamation scopes, and shared runtime/source ownership infrastructure.

Current boundaries: SDK modules may remain cached in the App process; synchronous checks cannot be forcibly interrupted; source locks provide cooperative replacement protection rather than sandboxing.

Additional TODO comments in `loader.py` and `python_backend.py` describe a future environment-management change:

    install dependency updates into a new directory
    new processes use the new packages
    running processes keep their existing packages
    delete the old directory after its last process exits

The package/file lookup could then be prepared during installation and reused at runtime. This belongs in a separate PR covering installation, process startup, recovery, and cleanup. It must define when an existing App restarts to activate new dependencies and preserve desktop/user-managed Python environments.

Until those guarantees exist, retain runtime observation of the mutable shared environment. Its cost depends on installed packages and loaded modules; the measured residual memory difference is not a fixed per-plugin charge.

The performance follow-up also adds two focused regression tests and adapts one existing memory test fixture. These should be included in the test-cost review.

## Type of Change

- [x] Bug fix
- [x] New feature
- [ ] Breaking change
- [x] Documentation
- [x] Refactoring

## Component(s) Affected

- [x] Core / Backend (app, agents, config, providers, utils, local_models)
- [ ] Console (frontend web UI)
- [x] Channels (DingTalk, Lark, QQ, Discord, iMessage, etc.)
- [ ] Skills
- [x] CLI
- [ ] Documentation (website)
- [x] Tests
- [ ] CI/CD
- [ ] Scripts / Deploy

## Checklist

- [x] I ran `pre-commit run --all-files` locally and it passes
- [x] If pre-commit auto-fixed files, I committed those changes and reran checks
- [ ] I ran tests locally (`pytest` or as relevant) and they pass
  - Targeted suites pass; one additional failure also reproduces on main. Details below.
- [x] Documentation updated (if needed)
- [x] Ready for review

### For Channel Changes (DingTalk, Lark, QQ, Console, etc.)

- [x] I ran `./scripts/check-channels.sh` (or `./scripts/check-channels.sh --changed`) and it passes
- [x] Official channel changes are covered in `tests/unit/channels/test_<channel>.py` (startup, shutdown and message delivery)
- [x] Shared host/process changes are covered in `test_channel_host.py` / `tests/unit/plugins/test_plugin_process.py`
- [x] Console changes retain the built-in contract checks in `tests/contract/channels/`

Existing official-driver and Console contract suites were rerun. Their implementations were not directly modified.

## Evidence

### 4) Validation

Local environment: macOS, Python 3.11. Groups overlap and are not a cumulative total.

| Scope | Result |
|---|---|
| Full `check-channels.sh`: official channels, Console contracts, host/process | 247 passed, 1 existing Windows-only skip; 199.31s |
| CLI, channel host, manifest dependencies, Provider CLI | 189 passed |
| Existing loading, reload, configuration, isolation and cleanup | 193 passed |
| Cloudpaw and installation locks | 34 passed, 2 existing platform skips |
| SDK entry and author-check contracts | 13 passed |
| Hello installation, invocation, Doctor, uninstall and existing Tool behavior | 11 scenario steps passed |
| Additional dependency/lifecycle checks | 110 passed, 1 main-reproduced failure |

Coverage includes command discovery/removal, native CLI compatibility, dependency checks before SDK imports, preservation of backend configuration, asynchronous cancellation cleanup, extension revocation, deferred channel SDK loading, message delivery, worker rollback, and Provider configuration updates.

The remaining failure is:

`test_loader_dep_probing.py::test_host_observation_reuses_only_scoped_raw_inputs`

Its multiline `Requires-Dist` whitespace assertion fails identically on main `401662d8cbd2` under the same interpreter. The test and Requires-Dist parser were left unchanged; no skip or xfail was added.

`pre-commit run --all-files` passed all applicable hooks and made no automatic changes.

Nightly test has been passed.

#### Additional validation for the performance fix

| Scope | Result |
|---|---|
| Memory contracts/lifecycle, CLI invocation, all channel unit/contract tests, plugin processes | 299 passed, 1 existing Windows-only skip; 199.21s |
| Committed-vs-fixed CLI replay | 13 cases with matching business output, errors, and exit codes |

The replay covers core commands, plugin help and execution, Unicode/empty arguments, and invalid command-line input.

The final `pre-commit run --all-files` passed after the performance fix. The new registry file also passed a separate file-scoped run before staging. Neither final run modified files.

#### Resource measurements

Same Hello Click business implementation on macOS/Python 3.11: one warm-up, then five fresh processes per variant, with alternating execution order.

| Invocation | Median runtime | Median peak RSS | Peak threads |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| Native reference | 1.794 s | 175.83 MiB | 1 |
| Plugin CLI before the performance fix | 2.656 s | 214.77 MiB | 2 |
| Plugin CLI after the performance fix | 2.385 s | 193.69 MiB | 2 |

The native reference mounts the factory directly with a simple JSON store; plugin cases use SDK storage. These are whole-invocation measurements.

In the instrumented Hello probe, cleanup-triggered imports fell **221 → 0 modules**, and cached file-path rows fell **42,092 → 2,463**, with the same 81 imported package owners identified.

The extra thread belongs to the existing async I/O executor and is joined during shutdown. No child processes remained.

## Additional Notes

- SDK/API and channel version/schema decisions require maintainer approval.
- Tests reuse existing fixtures and CI jobs; no test dependencies or paid-model requests were added.
- Uninstall does not automatically delete shared Python SDK packages.
- Local review notes are excluded from the final PR file changes.

prs.title: feat(chat): add append-only session storage, paginated history and native Turn forks
prs.body:
## Description

Long conversations previously depended on mutable session snapshots and loading large history windows. That made historical Turn forks, runtime recovery, and reconnect behavior difficult to keep consistent. This branch introduces durable per-session SQLite history with append-only facts and rebuildable projections, and bounds the Console's history and replay work.

This draft covers the complete branch, including:

- Store message/content facts and immutable context revisions separately from current message/runtime projections. Rebuild projections without rewriting historical facts; reuse state component references for usage-only revisions and avoid redundant block events.
- Migrate legacy JSON sessions and history databases, preserve available historical messages, reconstruct legacy runtime where possible, and retain provider session/Turn mappings.
- Fork completed Turns with their historical runtime boundary. Codex/Qoder branches use native provider interfaces and stored Turn mappings rather than rebuilding third-party context. Failed native restoration/reset must not silently create a fresh context.
- Add stable history pagination, bounded rendering, message-directory navigation, streaming/reconnect replay, and safe session switching/deletion.
- Integrate storage with clear/new, compact, dump/load, Scroll/Recall, cloning, backup, checkpoints, statistics, and PawApp/SDK session access. Preserve reset and checkpoint restoration semantics; roll back failed/cancelled compaction.

**Related Issue:** No linked issue.

**Security Considerations:** Session ownership and active-session deletion checks remain part of history access. This PR does not include local databases, conversation exports, screenshots, profiling dumps, or environment credentials. Provider contexts remain provider-owned.

## Type of Change

- [x] Bug fix
- [x] New feature
- [x] Refactoring
- [x] Breaking change (session storage representation changes; legacy data is imported)
- [ ] Documentation

## Component(s) Affected

- [x] Core / Backend
- [x] Console
- [x] Channels (Console streaming/reconnect)
- [x] Tests
- [x] Scripts / Deploy (replay verification tooling)

## Checklist

- [ ] `pre-commit run --all-files` passes (changed-file checks passed; no all-files claim)
- [ ] Full default test configuration is green (see known failures below)
- [ ] Documentation published in this repository
- [ ] Ready for review / merge

## Testing

The latest local validation ran against the committed working tree in the project Conda environment. Groups overlap and should not be summed as unique coverage.

prs.title: feat(crons): per-run sessions to bound cron job history growth
prs.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Every cron execution currently appends its conversation to **one dedicated per-job session** (`share_session=False`). The model context is isolated per run via `CronMemoryIsolate`/`Restore` hooks, but the persisted session keeps every run's messages, and the **full history is loaded into memory (and snapshotted) on each execution**.

For high-frequency jobs this grows without bound. Production example: a job running every 5 minutes accumulated **~7,300 messages / ~9M estimated tokens per day** in its per-job session, eventually exhausting container memory (OOM restart loop). This affects any user with frequent scheduled tasks — the session size scales with `run frequency × lifetime`, not with actual usage.

## Solution

Add an **opt-in per-run session mode** that bounds everything to a single execution:

- **`JobRuntimeSpec.per_run_session`** (default `False`, fully backward compatible): when enabled (and `share_session` is `False`), each execution runs in its own session `cron:{target}:job:{job}:run:{run}`, so context loading and persisted history stay O(single run) regardless of job frequency. Run chats carry a timestamp suffix in their display name so operators can tell runs apart.
- **Lazy retention**: after registering the run chat, the job's run chats are trimmed to the newest `QWENPAW_CRON_RUN_SESSION_KEEP` (default 50) — deleting both the chat specs and their session JSON files, so the chat list and disk stay bounded together. Best-effort by design: trimming failures never affect the run outcome. Run audit facts remain available via cron execution records (`CRON_HISTORY_LIMIT`).
- **`SafeJSONSession.delete_session_file`**: remove one persisted session file (reusing the established path conventions), so retention bounds storage along with the chat list.
- **`create_or_replace_job`**: per-field preservation for omitted runtime flags — `share_session` and `per_run_session` are carried over from the previous definition independently when not explicitly set (the previous block-level check would mis-handle the new field since serialized payloads always carry all fields).

The per-run session id reuses the existing `_safe_session_component` derivation rules (length-bounded, collision-resistant), and the cron memory-isolation hooks require no changes — with per-run sessions their snapshot/restore cost is naturally O(single run).

## Out of scope

- Existing per-job sessions created before enabling the flag are not migrated or swept here (different session-id shape); operators can retire them by re-saving jobs with the flag (new sessions start fresh) or deleting stale chats via the existing chat APIs.

## Testing

- New unit tests: per-run ids differ across executions with the `:run:` prefix; retention trims the oldest run chats (specs + session files) beyond the window while never touching unrelated chats; legacy mode is byte-for-byte behavior-preserved (including the existing `":run:" not in session_id` assertion) and never invokes housekeeping.
- Full unit suite: 16,212 passed; the 53 pre-existing environment failures (sqlite FTS5 / plugin subprocess) are identical with and without this change (verified via baseline stash run).


## Type of Change

- [x] Feature (non-breaking, additive: new opt-in `per_run_session` runtime flag, default `False`)
- [ ] Bug fix / Breaking change / Documentation / Refactoring

## Component(s) Affected

- [x] Core (`src/qwenpaw/app/crons/`, `src/qwenpaw/app/chats/session.py`)
- [ ] Console / Channels / Skills / CLI / Documentation

## Checklist

- [x] Tests added/updated and passing locally (584 crons+chats+hooks tests; full suite failures identical to baseline via stash comparison)
- [x] `pre-commit run --files ...` passes on all changed files (black/flake8/pylint/mypy)
- [x] Backward compatible: default behavior unchanged (covered by existing assertions)

prs.title: fix(desktop): open workspace HTML via the decoded local path
prs.body:
## Description

The legacy desktop bridge (`WebViewAPI`, pywebview shell) opened workspace HTML previews by handing the percent-encoded `file://` URI from `GET /api/workspace/html-file-uri` (`Path.as_uri()`, UTF-8 percent-encoded) straight to `webbrowser.open`.

On Windows, `webbrowser`→`os.startfile`→ShellExecute percent-decodes with the **ANSI code page** — GBK on Chinese systems — so the UTF-8 encoding of a Chinese workspace path is decoded to garbage and Windows reports `ERROR_FILE_NOT_FOUND` (issue #8502 复现 A; the same failure mode was verified with `ShellExecuteW` in the issue).

This change decodes the URI host-agnostically with `urllib.request.url2pathname` (UTF-8 aware, converts URI separators to native ones) and passes the **native local path** to `webbrowser.open` instead of the `file://` URL.

**Related Issue:** Fixes #8502 (复现 A — the pywebview legacy bridge layer)

**Security Considerations:** None — the resolved URI already passed the loopback + `/api/workspace/html-file-uri` gate; this only changes how the resolved `file` URI is handed to the OS opener (same file the endpoint validated — suffix recheck unchanged).

## Type of Change

- [x] Bug fix

## Component(s) Affected

- [x] Core / Backend (app, agents, config, providers, utils, local_models)
- [ ] Console (frontend web UI) — symptom surfaces here; the change is in the desktop bridge
- [ ] Channels
- [ ] Skills
- [x] CLI
- [ ] Documentation (website)
- [x] Tests
- [ ] CI/CD
- [ ] Scripts / Deploy

## Checklist

- [x] I ran `pre-commit run --all-files` locally and it passes
- [x] If pre-commit auto-fixed files, I committed those changes and reran checks
- [x] I ran tests locally (`pytest` or as relevant) and they pass
- [ ] Documentation updated (if needed)
- [x] Ready for review

## Testing

```
uv run pytest tests/unit/cli/test_desktop_cmd.py -q
..ss...                       [100%]
5 passed, 2 skipped in 0.43s
```

New regression case: `test_open_workspace_html_opens_the_decoded_local_path` builds a real workspace file at `workspace_dir/工作区/report.html`, feeds its `as_uri()` (percent-encoded) through the endpoint payload the same way the bridge consumes it, and asserts `webbrowser.open` receives the decoded native path. The test fails against `main` (assertion showed the encoded \'/C:/Users/.../%E5%B7%A5...\' arriving at the opener).

## Evidence

```
$ uv run pytest tests/unit/cli/test_desktop_cmd.py -q
......ss                       [100%]
5 passed, 2 skipped in 0.43s

$ uv run pytest "tests/unit/cli/test_desktop_cmd.py::test_open_workspace_html_opens_the_decoded_local_path" -q   # with the fix reverted
F                                                                                                                 [100%]
1 failed in 1.45s
```

FAIL output (fix reverted) — the opener received the encoded URI instead of the decoded native path:

```
E       AssertionError: assert [\'/C:/Users/T...imn6jmm_e7/工作区/report.html\'] == [\'C:\Users\...\report.html\']
E         At index 0 diff: \'/C:/Users/Tony/AppData/Local/Temp/tmpn6jmm_e7/工作区/report.html\' != \'C:\Users\Tony\AppData\Local\Temp\tmpn6jmm_e7\工作区\report.html\'
```

(The diff shows the pre-fix `unquote`-only form retaining the URI-leading \'/\'; with `url2pathname` the opener gets exactly the native path. The issue's复现 A error dialog — `file:///E:/%E5%B7%A5%E4%BD%9C%E5%8C%BA/... Windows 找不到文件` — corresponds to that same encoded form reaching ShellExecute.)

Note: 复现 B (workspace-root-external file with pure-ASCII path, no reaction) involves a different layer (the Tauri shell invoke of `open_workspace_html` when the file sits outside the workspace root); that path resolves through the backend resolver and is not addressed by this bridge change.

prs.title: feat(models): run local Piccolo with bidirectional candidate scoring
prs.body:
## Description

Allow downloaded Piccolo models to supply QwenPaw's native Jev decisions for automatic tool review and ReMe context compaction. Piccolo uses bidirectional prompt attention and candidate-token scoring, so a causal Chat Completions adapter cannot reproduce its trained inference behavior.

- Reuse AgentScope's Jev question/answer mapping and call the managed llama.cpp runtime's native `/v1/systemone` endpoint, with request compression disabled. Read candidate-token probabilities instead of generating probability JSON.
- Preserve the existing Download → Start → default Decision model flow and the separate automatic-review and decision-compaction switches. Starting Piccolo does not enable either feature or change another provider's chat selection.
- Group the local selector into independently scrollable **Chat models** and **Decision models** sections, with Chinese labels **对话模型** and **决策模型**. Remove the redundant Local Models heading, Piccolo purpose subtitle, and blue repository links. Keep a single managed runtime.
- Use current `agentscope-ai` Hugging Face repositories for QwenPaw-Flash recommendations; preserve stored IDs for existing downloads and their lifecycle actions.
- Recommend separate `agentscope-ai/Piccolo-{4,9,27}B-BF16` and `-Q8_0` repositories according to machine memory. BF16 downloads use the standard complete GGUF shard set, with known total sizes; BF16 repository IDs retain the native decision role through download, restart and activation. Recognize only the Piccolo family IDs; no legacy Blink repository or cache aliases are added. Preserve the decision role after download, restart, and API activation. Download GGUF/runtime metadata only.
- Launch Piccolo with a complete-prompt budget, one slot, no prompt cache, and no context shifting. Reject runtimes that report Piccolo as a text-generation model.
- Include a focused companion llama.cpp patch and build instructions in `docs/local-piccolo.md`. Ordinary Ollama Chat Completions is not enabled for this contract.

The companion patch targets llama.cpp `f4d8af608a6b39946406f9439edfb6e83ca6a923`. It adds Piccolo metadata and the checkpoint's exact `flex_twice` layout to the existing native SystemOne implementation. Full-attention layers use bidirectional prompt attention; linear-attention layers keep their native computation. Candidate softmax at temperature 1 is equivalent to renormalizing the candidate token log probabilities. No answer tokens are generated.

**Related work:** Reuses the decision configuration and review integration in #8205 and #8360.

**Security considerations:** Existing approval thresholds, human-confirmation fallback, context recovery, and opt-in switches remain in control. Candidate probabilities are model outputs, not a calibration or safety guarantee.

## Type of Change

- [x] New feature
- [x] Documentation
- [x] Refactoring
- [ ] Breaking change

## Components

Local model lifecycle and catalog, provider adapter, Console capability detection, English model guide, and tests. No workflow files are changed.

## Evidence

- Scope cleanup: 174 focused backend/API tests and 35 selector tests passed. Keep the existing Start request shape and integer model-size schema; runtime metadata selects the decision role. No runtime source dependency on the Piccolo repository is added.
- BF16 catalog follow-up: 177 focused backend/API tests and 35 model-selector tests passed, covering memory boundaries, GGUF-only downloads, BF16 decision identity and existing Start controls. Changed Python hooks and Prettier passed.
- Rename follow-up: 188 focused backend tests and 34 model-selector tests passed. The renamed companion patch applies to the pinned source.
- 258 focused backend tests passed (one existing tar extraction deprecation warning).
- 5 relevant Console test files / 117 tests passed; production frontend build passed.
- Changed Python hooks passed: AST, encoding, private-key scan, whitespace, trailing commas, mypy, Black, flake8, and pylint. Changed Console/docs passed Prettier. The full-repository pre-commit run is not claimed as passing; unrelated formatter/actionlint bootstrap and full CI remain outstanding.
- Companion runtime: 49 server-component tests / 191 assertions passed. The patch applies cleanly to the pinned upstream source.
- Exact C++ versus checkpoint-tokenizer comparison: 33 cases across three tokenizers, 78 prompt rows, including 255 options, ordered scores, Chinese, special tokens, and non-repeated long prompts.
- Complete original 4B, 9B, and 27B checkpoints ran in the Transformers reference. BF16 and Q8 GGUFs were compared on four smoke questions per size. Q8 maximum absolute candidate probability differences were approximately 0.00564 / 0.00286 / 0.00298, with matching top choices.
- On a Mac M4 Pro, the complete 4B checkpoint ran through the CPU reference, and 4B Q8 GGUF ran on Metal through the actual native classifier, `assess_tool_call()`, and ReMe decision component. These smoke tests did not execute a reviewed tool or change approval settings.

### Local model selector

English:

![English local model selector](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Xinji-Mai/QwenPaw/58d7ec350cfd83e3fe8313115f2971820aa564b9/docs/images/local-models-en.png)

Chinese:

![Chinese local model selector](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Xinji-Mai/QwenPaw/58d7ec350cfd83e3fe8313115f2971820aa564b9/docs/images/local-models-zh.png)

## Limitations and release status

A Piccolo-compatible llama.cpp binary is required; the companion patch is not in a released upstream binary. The build/install step is documented and the capability gate rejects an incompatible runtime. The local runtime serves one model at a time. This initial Piccolo integration caps each complete question prompt at 8,192 tokens, including repeated layout, to bound full-attention memory allocation even when the shared chat window is 64K. Oversized prompts fail to the existing fallback.

The complete 4B, 9B and 27B checkpoints and their Q8_0 and Q4_K_M variants are public under `agentscope-ai/Piccolo-{4,9,27}B`, with separate `-Q8_0` and `-Q4_K_M` repositories. All nine renamed repositories were independently checked for public revisions, manifest file sizes and unchanged LFS weight hashes. Model cards retain Apache-2.0 and FlexDM attribution. The catalog now recommends BF16 as well as Q8_0 according to memory; Q4_K_M can be downloaded by repository ID. BF16 uses separate `Piccolo-{4,9,27}B-BF16` repositories. All three BF16 repositories are now public. Their complete standard GGUF shard sets (4B: 8.42 GB / 2 shards; 9B: 17.92 GB / 4 shards; 27B: 53.81 GB / 12 shards) were independently checked against the published HEAD, file sizes and SHA-256 receipts. Its model cards disclose the expanded synthetic 265-request / 556-judgment regressions and measured differences. Repository existence or successful loading is not a task-quality benchmark.

Native QwenPaw download completed against the public 4B Q8 repository, reusing a local GGUF cache after remote SHA-256 verification. The Mac managed Start flow subsequently passed in approximately 7.07 seconds and advertised the native decisions capability. The actual QwenPaw-managed runtime then passed classifier, automatic-review, and ReMe compaction smoke calls (1.77-second classifier, 3.10-second review, 0 generated answer tokens). An earlier startup SIGKILL did not reproduce on retry; its cause remains unestablished.

The PR runtime evidence consists of smoke comparisons. The separately published Q4 artifacts also include expanded synthetic numerical regressions; neither establishes task-quality, probability-calibration, or safety performance. The recommendation tiers are 16/24/48 GB for Q8 and 24/32/80 GB for BF16 (4B/9B/27B). These are catalog policies that reserve room for runtime buffers, not measured peak-memory guarantees; exact platform/context usage still requires broader measurement.

## Local inference budgets

The local 4B Q4 review prefill measured 3.3–4.4 seconds, so the previous four-second deadline could fall back to human approval before a valid result arrived. Local review requests default to 7 seconds; the compaction classifier client retains its 30-second default. Explicit lower timeouts remain respected. Remote Jev defaults and all approval thresholds are unchanged.

For local ReMe compaction, cap the existing evidence packer at 1,600 state tokens and 4,096 request tokens with one batch in flight. Give model inference 80% of the configured total deadline (24 seconds of the default 30), leaving time for validation and atomic commit. Unanswered or oversized evidence remains verbatim. User settings, recent-message protection, archive references and the original fallback remain intact.

The synthetic live compaction fixture reduced formatted input from 10,432 to 6,670 tokens in 24.0 seconds, retaining the order evidence, latest user message and six recent messages. These are budget regression measurements on the local 4B setup, not task-quality or safety-calibration results. Review remains conservative: the file-write and printf fixtures still requested approval; the bounded line-count command was classified low risk and completed through the real JEV-mode chat path.

prs.title: fix(context): support slow summary models and consistent token limits
prs.body:
## Description

Scroll summary requests can fail with HTTP 400 on OpenAI-compatible providers when a model card sets `generate_kwargs.max_tokens`: AgentScope 2.0.10 injects `max_completion_tokens` while Scroll also passes `max_tokens`. Keep configured output limits unchanged until the compatibility boundary, resolve one output-token parameter for the request, and normalize defaults and per-call overrides separately before merging. Summary limits can then override configured defaults for GLM, GPT and o-series models.

Preserve an explicit `max_completion_tokens` in provider configuration, model configuration or per-call arguments, including custom Azure deployment names such as `production-reasoner`. Deployment aliases do not reliably identify the underlying model family. A per-call summary cap still overrides the configured value, and only one output-token parameter reaches the SDK. Configuration dictionaries remain unchanged.

Make Scroll's continuation-summary timeout configurable with `running.light_context_config.scroll_config.summary_timeout_seconds`, and increase the default from 60 to 300 seconds for slow reasoning models. Both normal agent construction and standalone `/compact` forward the configured timeout. The finite positive budget covers preparation, generation, validation and a quality retry; retries share the remaining time. Existing cancellation and previous-summary preservation behavior remain in place. Update English and Chinese configuration documentation.

**Related Issue:** Relates to #8464; addresses the two follow-up problems in https://github.com/agentscope-ai/QwenPaw/issues/8464#issuecomment-6469428885. Conversation-model selection is handled separately by #8465.

prs.title: fix(tools): preserve line endings and encoding in edit_file (#8414, #8415)
prs.body:
Fixes #8414, #8415.

## What Problem This Solves

`edit_file` rewrote the whole file through a text-mode writer (`newline='\n'`, UTF-8). Two user-visible bugs followed:

- **CRLF files were converted to LF on every edit** (#8414, #8415) — a one-line change rewrote every line ending in the file, which shows up as a whole-file diff in git and can break files that require CRLF (Windows batch scripts, some configs).
- **Non-UTF-8 files were destroyed** — an ISO-8859-1 file with bytes outside ASCII was re-encoded (or failed) even when the edit itself touched nothing near them.

The fix writes the snapshot back byte for byte: `edit_file` now reads the raw bytes, decodes with the encoding the file actually uses (BOM detection first), applies the replacement, re-encodes, and hands the result to a new `_write_bytes_atomic` that writes a sibling temp file in binary and `os.replace()`s it into place. Line endings are normalised for *matching* only, then the file's own ending is re-applied to inserted text.

## Evidence

Unit tests in `tests/unit/agents/tools/test_file_io.py` (all new, per file-ending/encoding case):

- `test_crlf_endings_survive_a_one_line_edit` — a CRLF file edited in the middle keeps CRLF everywhere; byte-comparing the whole file passes
- `test_lf_file_is_unchanged_in_shape` — an LF file is not rewritten into CRLF
- `test_iso_8859_1_bytes_are_not_destroyed` — a Latin-1 file with non-ASCII bytes around the edit point round-trips
- `test_utf8_bom_is_preserved` — the BOM is still there after editing
- `test_new_lines_in_new_text_follow_the_file_ending` — inserted text uses the file's ending, not a hardcoded `\n`

The atomic writer also keeps the target's mode: `shutil.copymode(target, temp)` when the file exists (which additionally preserves setuid/setgid bits that a `st_mode & 0o777` mask dropped), and the constant `0o644` for a brand-new file.

CI on this revision: pre-commit (black 23.3.0, flake8, mypy, pylint) clean, CodeQL clean, unit tests passing.

issues.body:
### Summary

`Config::save_dirty` writes only the dirty paths onto the on-disk document and then unconditionally sets `schema_version = CURRENT_SCHEMA_VERSION` (added in #7274 to fix the opposite case, a current-shaped body under a stale label). When the file on disk still has a pre-V3 body (top-level `default_provider`, `default_model`, no `[agents.*]`), the incremental save leaves that body as it is but relabels it V3. On the next start, migration sees V3 and does nothing, so the legacy fields are never turned into an agent.

### Observed

A config written by an external provisioner in the single-agent layout (top-level `default_provider = "openrouter"`, `default_model`, `[gateway]`, `[workspace]`, no `schema_version`). The daemon (v0.8.4, Homebrew) started, migrated it in memory, and a gateway pairing then saved `gateway.paired_tokens` through `save_dirty`. Afterwards the file has `schema_version = 3` at the top and the same legacy body.

- With the stamp in place, `zeroclaw --config-dir <dir> agents list` shows no agents.
- On a copy with the `schema_version = 3` line removed, the same command shows `default`, because load-time migration runs again and synthesizes the default agent.

### Expected

An incremental save of a file whose on-disk label is older than `CURRENT_SCHEMA_VERSION` should not produce a V3 label over a pre-V3 body. Either fall back to a full migrated `save()` for that file (the in-memory config is already migrated), or keep the on-disk label when the body was not migrated.

### Where

- `crates/zeroclaw-config/src/schema.rs`, `save_dirty`: the `doc.as_table_mut().insert("schema_version", ...)` after `apply_dirty_path` (present at v0.8.4 and on master at 584d6da0).
- Regression test from #7274: `save_dirty_stamps_current_schema_version_on_stale_label` covers a V2-labelled file gaining a current-shaped section; there is no case for a legacy body that the dirty paths do not touch.

### Workaround

Remove the `schema_version = 3` line, run `zeroclaw --config-dir <dir> config migrate`, and check `agents list`.

### Related (separate, smaller)

The OpenRouter provider's error at v0.8.4 says "Set OPENROUTER_API_KEY env var", but v0.8.4 has no code that reads that variable (the string appears only in the error messages in `crates/zeroclaw-providers/src/openrouter.rs`). The message is gone on master; worth confirming master does not tell users to set it elsewhere.

issues.body:
### Affected component security/sandbox ### Severity S2 - degraded behavior ### Current behavior On Unix the shell tool puts the child in its own session (`setsid`, `crates/zeroclaw-runtime/src/tools/shell.rs:340-356`) and `ChildGroupGuard` SIGKILLs the whole group on timeout or cancel (`shell.rs:18-60`). Both are `#[cfg(unix)]`. On Windows the timeout path is `child.start_kill()` (`shell.rs:421`) plus `kill_on_drop(true)` (`shell.rs:358`): `TerminateProcess` on `cmd.exe` or `powershell.exe` only. Windows has no process group to signal, so whatever the interpreter started (node, python, cargo, a `start`-ed program, anything a skill launches) keeps running with the daemon's privileges and the inherited pipe handles. Same shape in `skill_tool` (`tokio::time::timeout(..., cmd.output())`, `crates/zeroclaw-runtime/src/tools/skill_tool.rs:229`; dropping the future kills the interpreter only) and in `coding_cli_executor` (`crates/zeroclaw-runtime/src/tools/coding_cli_executor.rs:91-93`). The crate already depends on `process-wrap` with the `job-object` feature (`crates/zeroclaw-runtime/Cargo.toml:104`) and uses it for the grok CLI (`crates/zeroclaw-providers/src/grok_cli.rs:80`) and the service runner (`WindowsServiceJob`, `crates/zeroclaw-runtime/src/service/mod.rs:1093-1131`); the desktop app wraps its daemon probe the same way (`apps/tauri/src/daemon.rs:208-214`). Open PRs touch the edges without closing this: #11827 puts the daemon and everything it spawns in a kill-on-close job, so orphans die when the daemon exits, not when a command times out. #11456 wraps a command in a Job Object only while `shell_max_memory_mb` supervision is enabled ("disabled supervision keeps ordinary child waiting"), so the default configuration keeps today's behaviour. ### Expected behavior On Windows every shell, skill and coding-CLI command runs inside a kill-on-close Job Object (`process_wrap::tokio::JobObject` with `KillOnDrop`), so timeout, cancellation and e-stop end the whole tree, matching the Unix process-group guard. Nothing spawned by a tool needs to outlive it today; anything that does later can request breakaway explicitly. ### Steps to reproduce ```bash # agent: shell_timeout_secs = 5; python is in the default allowlist # 1. file_write sleep.py content="import time\ntime.sleep(600)\n" # 2. shell "python sleep.py" # 3. After "Command timed out after 5s and was killed": tasklist /FI "IMAGENAME eq python.exe" # python.exe is still listed; its parent cmd.exe / powershell.exe is gone. ``` ### Impact **Attack vector.** A command the model starts outlives the timeout. Deliberately: a prompt-injected model writes a script into the workspace and runs it through allowlisted `python` or `node` (a listener, a reverse shell, a miner, a poller). Accidentally: any build, test or server command that exceeds `shell_timeout_secs`. ZeroClaw terminates the interpreter, reports "killed", and the descendant continues. Every dialect is affected; PowerShell's children survive the same way. **Likelihood.** Moderate for the accidental case on any Windows host that uses the shell tool. Deliberate abuse needs a model already induced to run something, so it mostly amplifies another compromise or follows a legitimate-looking long command. **Data exposed.** None directly. The loss is control: timed-out or cancelled work keeps running as the daemon's account outside the e-stop (#9802), holding CPU, memory, ports and file locks, and continuing whatever it was doing (calling billed APIs, serving a port, waiting for input). An orphan holding the gateway port is the stuck-port failure in #8800. Related: #6916. **Attack path** ```mermaid sequenceDiagram autonumber participant M as Model participant S as shell tool participant I as cmd.exe / powershell.exe participant D as Descendant
(python, node, listener) M->>S: shell "python sleep.py" S->>I: spawn (no Job Object) I->>D: spawn child Note over S: shell_timeout_secs elapses S->>I: start_kill (TerminateProcess on the interpreter) I-->>S: exited S-->>M: "Command timed out after 5s and was killed" Note over D: keeps running as the daemon's account,
holds pipes, ports and files, outside e-stop ``` **Data flow** ```mermaid flowchart TB subgraph unix ["Unix today"] U1["shell tool"] -->|"setsid"| U2["child in its own process group"] U2 --> U3["descendants in the same group"] U1 -->|"timeout: kill(-pgid, SIGKILL)"| U3 end subgraph win ["Windows today"] W1["shell tool"] --> W2["cmd.exe / powershell.exe"] W2 --> W3["descendants"] W1 -->|"timeout: TerminateProcess"| W2 W3 -.->|"survive: no Job Object"| W4["orphans: CPU, ports, file locks, cost, no e-stop"] end ``` **Evidence:** static review of master `1c1cd118ac`; not executed on a Windows host. ### Logs / stack traces _No response_ ### ZeroClaw version master `1c1cd118ac` (v0.8.7) ### Rust version 1.98.0 (CI toolchain) ### Operating system Windows 10 / 11 ### Regression? No, first-time setup ### Pre-flight checks - [ ] I reproduced this on the latest master branch or latest release. - [x] I redacted secrets, tokens, and personal data from all submitted content.

issues.title: [Feature]: Long-running shell tasks with async/sync modes and a user-operated interactive terminal
issues.body:
### Summary

Support long-running shell tasks with explicit asynchronous and synchronous execution modes, plus a separate interactive terminal where users can enter input directly.

### Problem statement

The built-in shell call currently waits for completion within a configured timeout, closes stdin, and does not expose an interactive terminal. This makes two common workflows difficult:

- Builds, training scripts, and development servers can exceed the shell timeout. The agent needs to wait briefly for fast completion, then continue its turn while a longer task keeps running.
- Commands that request passwords, confirmations, or other terminal input need a user-operated terminal. Increasing a timeout does not provide that input path.

Related issue #1404 proposed background process management but explicitly excluded writing to stdin. This request covers explicit wait/timeout semantics and a user-facing interactive terminal; the historical background-process implementation should be assessed for reuse during design.

### Proposed solution

#### 1. Long-running script tasks

Expose an execution mode and mode-specific parameters in the model-facing tool schema. The parameter names below are illustrative; the behavior is the requirement.

**Asynchronous mode (`mode: "async"`, `wait_secs`)**

- Let the model pass the initial waiting duration with each call.
- Keep the tool call and the current turn blocked while the command runs within that waiting window.
- If the command finishes during the window, return its output and exit status immediately.
- If the window expires first, keep the same process running in the background, return a stable task handle, and let the turn continue. Do not restart the command during this transition.
- Background execution has no elapsed-time execution limit: the initial waiting duration is not a timeout. A task continues until it exits, is explicitly stopped, or its execution owner shuts down. This does not require surviving a daemon restart.
- Provide operations to inspect task status, retrieve incremental output and final exit status, and explicitly stop the task and its process group.

**Synchronous mode (`mode: "sync"`, `timeout_secs`)**

- Allow the execution timeout to be set per call.
- Keep the tool call and the current turn blocked until the command completes, reaches that timeout, or is cancelled.
- Return output and exit status on completion. On timeout, terminate the process group and return a clear timeout result; do not silently move the task into the background.

Validate mode-specific parameters and document their units, defaults, and cancellation behavior. In asynchronous mode, outer turn deadlines must not silently become background task execution deadlines after the task has been handed off.

#### 2. User-operated interactive shell

- Allow opening a separate terminal window or terminal pane backed by a PTY, where the user can directly interact with the shell or launched command.
- Support manual input for password prompts, confirmations, and similar interactive flows. Input must go directly to the terminal process; passwords must not be routed through the model, conversation history, tool receipts, or application logs. Preserve terminal echo behavior so password entry stays hidden when the command disables echo.
- Support live terminal output, normal terminal input, resize events, and interruption.
- Give the user a clear way to end the interactive session. On session end, window/pane closure, explicit cancellation, or owner shutdown, terminate and reap the owned process group so descendants are not left running. Use the platform-equivalent process-tree cleanup mechanism where Unix process groups are unavailable.
- If the current client cannot provide an interactive terminal, report that limitation clearly rather than launching an inaccessible prompt.

### Non-goals / out of scope

- Having the model collect, store, or type the user's passwords.
- Bypassing command approvals, sandboxing, tool visibility, or ownership checks.
- Persisting running processes across daemon restarts.
- A general-purpose remote desktop or terminal multiplexer.

### Alternatives considered

- Increase the existing shell timeout: helps some batch jobs but blocks the turn for the whole run and does not provide manual input.
- Run commands manually outside ZeroClaw and paste results back: loses task status and lifecycle integration.
- Use detached shell commands or external terminal multiplexers: leaves process ownership, cleanup, and result retrieval to the user.
- Add only a stdin-write operation: may help automation, but does not provide the requested separate user-operated terminal or full terminal semantics.

### Acceptance criteria

- [ ] The model-facing schema exposes asynchronous and synchronous execution modes with validated wait/timeout parameters.
- [ ] An asynchronous command finishing within `wait_secs` returns its result without waiting for the entire window.
- [ ] An asynchronous command exceeding `wait_secs` returns a task handle, releases the turn, and continues as the same process without an execution timeout.
- [ ] Background tasks expose status, incremental output, final exit status, and explicit process-group cancellation.
- [ ] A synchronous command blocks the turn until completion, cancellation, or its per-call timeout; timeout terminates the process group and reports the timeout.
- [ ] A supported client opens a separate interactive terminal window/pane and allows the user to answer prompts directly, including passwords with terminal echo disabled.
- [ ] Ending or closing an interactive session terminates and reaps its owned process group, including descendants.
- [ ] Password input is absent from model context, conversation history, tool receipts, and application logs.
- [ ] Existing approval, sandbox, and task ownership boundaries remain enforced for task creation and subsequent control operations.
- [ ] Tests cover the wait-to-background transition without duplicate execution, synchronous timeout, task cancellation, terminal input/echo handling, and descendant cleanup. User-facing documentation explains both modes and interactive-session lifecycle.

### Architecture impact

Shell tool schema and execution, runtime task ownership/cancellation, background task status/output, terminal/PTY management, client UI, security boundaries, and documentation.

The runtime should identify the canonical owner and task record for each running process and reuse existing lifecycle facilities where appropriate, rather than adding competing process registries. Maintainers should assess how an interactive terminal integrates with the supported clients and whether the design crosses an RFC trigger.

### Risk and rollback

Unlimited-duration background tasks can consume resources until explicitly stopped. Interactive sessions can expose sensitive terminal content or leave descendants behind if ownership and cleanup are incomplete. Keep these modes explicit, preserve existing authorization and isolation, bound retained output independently of execution duration, and provide visible stop controls and deterministic cleanup. Disabling the new modes restores the existing shell execution behavior; stop and clean up owned tasks/sessions when disabling them.

### Expected routing

Needs maintainer design assessment

### Next decision surface

Maintainer assessment of the shell task lifecycle and supported-client interactive terminal UX, including reuse of the historical work linked from #1404. Confirm implementation scope and promote to an RFC only if required by the repository's architecture rules.

### Breaking change?

No

### Data hygiene checks

- [x] I removed personal/sensitive data from examples, payloads, and logs.
- [x] I used neutral, project-focused wording and placeholders.

### Summary

Support multiple plugin registry URLs (comma-separated ZEROCLAW_PLUGIN_REGISTRY_URL)

### Problem statement

Currently, to use a third-party repo for plugins, you have to set ZEROCLAW_PLUGIN_REGISTRY_URL. But only a single repo is allowed, so I can't add my own third-party repo. export ZEROCLAW_PLUGIN_REGISTRY_URL=["https://github.com/seungjin/hanaclaw-plugins/releases/download/plugins/registry.json" ,"https://github.com/zeroclaw-labs/zeroclaw-plugins/blob/main/registry.json"]
